summary.text: At 56 and 60 the triples coincide: both are \((92,4,2)\), since their arithmetic derivatives are 92, their gcds with the arguments are 4, and exactly \(1^1\) and \(2^2\) divide them.  Both numbers are divisible by \(2^2\), so the original auxiliary function instead assigns them the distinct values 56 and 60; a finite first-appearance count through 60 therefore gives labels 42 and 40, respectively, at \(n=60\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
D(n)=A003415(n)=\sum_{p\mid n}v_p(n)\frac np,
\qquad
G(n)=A085731(n)=\gcd(D(n),n),
\]
and let
\[
C(n)=A376418(n)=\#\{k\geq 1:k^k\mid n\}.
\]
Also let \(Q(n)=1\) when no prime \(p\) satisfies \(p^p\mid n\), and let \(Q(n)=0\) otherwise. Equivalently, if
\(n=\prod p^{e_p}\), then \(Q(n)=0\) exactly when \(e_p\geq p\) for at least one prime \(p\).

The values used to define A379240 belong to the disjoint union of scalar values and pair values. Thus define
\[
F(n)=
\begin{cases}
\operatorname{pair}(D(n),G(n)),&Q(n)=1,\\
\operatorname{scalar}(n),&Q(n)=0.
\end{cases}
\]
The tags “pair” and “scalar” matter: a scalar can never equal a pair. The sequence A379240 is the restricted growth transform of \(F\).

For any sequence \(x(1),x(2),\ldots\), its restricted growth transform \(R_x\) labels the distinct values in order of first appearance. More precisely, list the distinct members of
\(x(1),\ldots,x(n)\), retaining their first-occurrence order. Then \(R_x(n)\) is the one-based position of \(x(n)\) in that list. In particular, if \(x(n)\) is a new value and exactly \(r\) distinct values have appeared before it, then \(R_x(n)=r+1\); if it appeared first at an earlier index \(m\), then \(R_x(n)=R_x(m)\).

The conjectured sequence is instead the restricted growth transform of
\[
T(n)=(D(n),G(n),C(n)).
\]
We will show that the two transforms disagree at \(n=60\).

First, all data needed up to 60 can be found directly from prime factorizations. For \(n\leq60\), the only possible nontrivial powers \(p^p\) dividing \(n\) are
\[
2^2=4\quad\text{and}\quad 3^3=27,
\]
since \(5^5>60\), and likewise \(p^p>60\) for every prime \(p\geq5\). Hence
\[
Q(n)=0\iff 4\mid n\ \text{or}\ 27\mid n
\qquad(1\le n\le60).
\]
The exceptional indices are therefore
\[
4,8,12,16,20,24,27,28,32,36,40,44,48,52,54,56,60.
\]

There is a similarly short determination of \(C(n)\). The value \(k=1\) always contributes. For \(k\geq4\), one has \(k^k\geq4^4=256>60\). Thus only \(k=2\) and \(k=3\) can make an additional contribution. No positive integer at most 60 is divisible by both 4 and 27, because their least common multiple is 108. Consequently,
\[
C(n)=
\begin{cases}
2,&4\mid n\text{ or }27\mid n,\\
1,&\text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\qquad(1\le n\le60).
\]

The column \(q\) is \(Q(n)\), \(r_F\) is the restricted-growth label of \(F(n)\), and \(r_T\) is that of \(T(n)\). Each \(D(n)\) is obtained from the displayed factorization by summing \(e(n/p)\) over its prime powers \(p^e\); \(G(n)\) is then an ordinary gcd. The last two columns result from scanning downward and either reusing the label of the first identical tagged value or triple, or assigning the next unused label.

Here is a direct explanation of the decisive final portion of the table. At 56,
\[
D(56)=3\frac{56}{2}+\frac{56}{7}=3\cdot28+8=92,
\]
so
\[
G(56)=\gcd(92,56)=4.
\]
Moreover, \(4\mid56\), while \(27\nmid56\), so \(Q(56)=0\) and \(C(56)=2\). Therefore
\[
F(56)=\operatorname{scalar}(56),
\qquad
T(56)=(92,4,2).
\]
The scan of indices 1 through 55 in the table contains exactly 39 distinct values of each kind, and neither \(\operatorname{scalar}(56)\) nor \((92,4,2)\) occurred earlier. Hence both receive label 40 at index 56.

At 57, the value is new in both transforms and receives label 41. At 58, one has
\((D,G,C)=(31,1,1)\), already seen at 30, and the corresponding pair value of \(F\) was likewise seen at 30, so both labels are 21. At 59, both values repeat the value first seen at a prime index, hence both labels are 2. Thus immediately before index 60, the original transform has seen 41 distinct \(F\)-values.

Now use
\[
60=2^2\cdot3\cdot5.
\]
Its arithmetic derivative value is
\[
D(60)=2\frac{60}{2}+\frac{60}{3}+\frac{60}{5}
      =2\cdot30+20+12
      =92,
\]
and therefore
\[
G(60)=\gcd(92,60)=4.
\]
Since \(4\mid60\), we have \(Q(60)=0\). Also \(k=1,2\) contribute to \(C(60)\), while \(3^3=27\nmid60\) and every \(k^k\) for \(k\ge4\) exceeds 60. Thus \(C(60)=2\).

Consequently,
\[
F(60)=\operatorname{scalar}(60),
\qquad
T(60)=(92,4,2).
\]
The scalar value \(\operatorname{scalar}(60)\) cannot have appeared at any earlier index. Indeed, pair-valued terms are in the other part of the disjoint union, and an earlier scalar-valued term at index \(m\) equals \(\operatorname{scalar}(m)\), which cannot be \(\operatorname{scalar}(60)\) when \(m<60\). Since 41 distinct \(F\)-values had appeared through index 59, this new value gets the next label:
\[
A379240(60)=R_F(60)=42.
\]

On the other hand,
\[
T(60)=(92,4,2)=T(56).
\]
Its first occurrence is at 56, where its restricted-growth label is 40. Therefore the conjectured triple transform reuses that label:
\[
R_T(60)=R_T(56)=40.
\]
We have thus obtained
\[
A379240(60)=42\neq40=R_T(60).
\]
Hence A379240 is not equal, term by term, to the restricted growth transform of
\([A003415(n),A085731(n),A376418(n)]\). The asserted universal equality is false.
